summaries.summary: Accurate language identification (LID) is the first step in many natural language processing and machine comprehension pipelines, enabling appropriate downstream models.
LID is important for harvesting scarce language resources, but data availability remains a major roadblock for supervised machine learning in developing countries.
Having 11 official languages of South Africa has improved resource availability, yet many South African languages remain under resourced for data driven models.
Table TABREF2 shows first language speaker percentages for South Africa's official languages, including similar Nguni and Sotho language groups.
This paper presents a hierarchical naive Bayesian and lexicon based classifier for LID of short text of 15-20 characters long.
Section SECREF2 reviews existing works, Section SECREF3 discusses the proposed algorithm, and Section SECREF4 presents comparative results.
This section focuses on recently published datasets and LID research applicable to the South African context, with a broader survey in BIBREF0.

The DSL 2015 & DSL 2017 shared tasks datasets are common LID benchmarks, with the 2017 dataset containing 14 languages, 6 language groups, 18000 training samples and 1000 testing samples per language.
JW300 covers over 300 languages with around 100 thousand parallel sentences per language pair, while WiLI-2018 includes around 1000 paragraphs of 235 languages.
The NCHLT text corpora can provide 3500 training samples and 600 testing samples of 300+ character sentences per language for South African languages.
Existing South African NLP resources include an LID algorithm using a character level n-gram language model, while shallow naive Bayes, SVMs and fasttext work well for LID.
Hierarchical stacked classifiers, surname classification between Tshivenda, Xitsonga and Sepedi, data augmentation and adversarial training are discussed as related approaches.
Deeper LID models include bidirectional recurrent neural networks and recurrent neural network ensembles, with the latter reported to achieve 95.12% in the DSL 2015 shared task.

LID of short texts, informal styles and similar languages remains difficult, while shallow methods work well and research opportunities include data harvesting, standardised datasets and shared tasks.
The proposed LID algorithm applies a naive Bayesian classifier with character (2, 4 & 6)-grams, word unigram and word bigram features with a hierarchical lexicon based classifier.
The naive Bayesian classifier first classifies text into Nguni, Sotho, English, Afrikaans, Xitsonga or Tshivenda using scikit-learn multinomial naive Bayes with alpha 0.01 and hashed text features.
The lexicon based classifier predicts the specific language within Nguni and Sotho groups, using high-confidence lexicon results or otherwise the naive Bayesian classifier's prediction.
The lexicon based classifier trades higher precision for lower recall and is confident when the winning language has at least one more word than second place.

The stacked classifier is tested against three public LID implementations, including fasttext with character (5-6)-gram features, 16 dimensional vectors, and LanideNN with learning rates 0.001 and 0.0001.
The stacked classifier is also tested against four other algorithms using the NCHLT, DSL 2015 and DSL 2017 datasets.
Table TABREF9 summarises average classification accuracy for specific language labels, while classifying text by language group or family is much easier.
Evaluated classifier variations include NB, NB+NB, NB+Lex, Lex, and a lexicon with 50% training token dropout.
DSL 2017 may be harder than DSL 2015 and NCHLT, and low BIBREF23 results are expected on shorter NCHLT-derived texts.
The proposed algorithm's accuracy depends on lexicon support, and without a good lexicon a non-stacked naive Bayesian classifier might perform better.
Table TABREF10 shows execution performance on an early 2015 13-inch Retina MacBook Pro with a 2.9 GHz CPU, 3.4 GHz Turbo Boost and 8GB RAM.
The proposed algorithm was evaluated on three existing datasets, compared with three public LID implementations and four other algorithms, and performed well but depends on lexicon support.
Future work includes investigating lexicon value and maintenance using self-supervised learning, deeper language models, and data augmentation strategies.
Further research opportunities include data harvesting, standardised datasets and shared tasks for South Africa and the rest of Africa.
